question: What is the main difference between endocrine and exocrine glands?

options.A: Exocrine glands have no connection to epithelial surfaces.
options.B: Endocrine glands rely exclusively on ducts to release secretions.
options.C: Exocrine glands produce hormones instead of enzymes.
options.D: Endocrine glands secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream.

explanation: Ductless endocrine glands release their chemical messengers straight into capillaries, whereas exocrine glands use ducts to empty substances onto surfaces. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why do endocrine responses usually take longer than nervous system responses?

options.A: Nerves use chemical neurotransmitters instead of electrical impulses.
options.B: Hormones require direct contact with target cell surface proteins.
options.C: Endocrine organs process stimuli much slower than spinal nerves.
options.D: Hormones must travel through the circulatory system to reach targets.

explanation: Circulating blood carries hormones across the body, which takes more time than electrical signals moving along a nerve cell. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h1)

question: Which structure connects the nervous system to the endocrine system?
explanation: The hypothalamus receives signals from the brain and turns them into hormonal messages to control the pituitary gland. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h2)

question: Which hormones are stored and released by the posterior pituitary gland?
explanation: Special cells in the hypothalamus make oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone, and send them down to be stored in the posterior pituitary. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h2)

question: Which dietary element is needed to make thyroid hormones?
explanation: The thyroid gland needs iodine to build working thyroxine and triiodothyronine molecules. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h3)

question: What is the main job of parathyroid hormone?

options.C: To promote sodium and water excretion

explanation: Parathyroid hormone acts on bones, kidneys, and the gut to bring calcium levels back up when they drop too low. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which hormone is the main mineralocorticoid released by the adrenal cortex?
explanation: Aldosterone helps balance electrolytes by telling the kidneys to hold onto sodium and get rid of potassium. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h4)

question: How does the adrenal medulla work differently from the adrenal cortex?

options.A: The medulla responds rapidly to acute stress through neural stimulation.
options.B: The medulla secretes steroid hormones necessary for long-term survival.
options.C: The medulla relies entirely on anterior pituitary tropic signals.
options.D: The medulla regulates serum calcium instead of blood glucose.

explanation: Nerves from the sympathetic nervous system connect directly to the adrenal medulla to trigger an instant release of stress hormones like adrenaline. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which specific cells in the pancreas make insulin?
explanation: Insulin is produced and released by the beta cells found inside the Islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is the main action of glucagon in the body?

options.A: To increase blood glucose by breaking down stored glycogen
options.B: To suppress the production of digestive enzymes in the gut
options.C: To promote cellular glucose uptake in skeletal muscles
options.D: To stimulate fat storage in adipose tissue depots

explanation: Glucagon tells the liver to break down stored sugar (glycogen) and release it into the blood when blood sugar levels are low. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h5)

question: Which hormone does the pineal gland release to help control sleep cycles?
explanation: The pineal gland makes more melatonin when it gets dark outside, signaling to the body that it is time to sleep. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h6)

question: What is the main job of Leydig cells in the male reproductive system?
explanation: Leydig cells inside the testes make and release testosterone when signaled by luteinizing hormone. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h6)

question: How does a negative feedback loop work in the endocrine system?

options.A: It continuously increases hormone production until medical intervention occurs.
options.B: It suppresses further hormone release when target levels become too high.
options.C: It speeds up metabolic pathways regardless of circulating hormone concentrations.
options.D: It reverses nervous system signals without involving chemical messengers.

explanation: Negative feedback acts like a thermostat, slowing down hormone production once levels reach the right amount. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h7)

question: Which situation is an example of a positive feedback mechanism in the body?

options.A: Insulin lowering blood glucose levels after a carbohydrate-rich meal
options.B: Aldosterone causing renal sodium reabsorption to raise blood pressure
options.C: Oxytocin release intensifying uterine contractions during labor
options.D: Thyroid hormone suppressing thyroid-stimulating hormone secretion

explanation: Childbirth uses positive feedback because the stretching of the cervix causes more oxytocin to be released, which makes contractions even stronger. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T1#GNS211_U1_T1_h7)
